title: Greetings and Their Replies
description: Twelve greetings you will hear in the first ten seconds of any Gulf encounter, each heard with its fixed reply before you ever say it. The reply is the lesson.
approach: GPA Phase 1 — receptive first. Every greeting is heard as a pair (greeting → reply) with two speakers on screen; the learner taps the reply that fits. Production is optional shadowing at the end.
can_do: Greet someone and answer their greeting
Say good morning, good evening and goodbye
Ask how someone is and say you are fine

culture.title: The reply is the lesson
culture.note: In the Gulf almost every greeting has a fixed answer, and the answer is not optional. السلام عليكم is returned word for word as وعليكم السلام; صباح الخير gets صباح النور; هلا gets هلا فيك or هلا والله. Greetings also come in chains — three or four in a row before anyone says anything else — so the safest habit is to give the reply, then send one greeting back (شلونك؟ … وإنت؟). Silence after a greeting reads as rudeness, not shyness.

culture.title: Right hand, then the chain
culture.note: Men shake with the right hand, often holding the handshake through the whole greeting chain; close friends add a cheek kiss, and in the Emirates and Qatar men may touch noses. A man greets a woman verbally unless she offers her hand first. Between women, a kiss on each cheek is normal. Whatever the gesture, the words come in the same order: peace greeting, هلا, how are you, how are things — then the actual conversation.

phrases.english: How are you? How are things?

vocabulary.teaching_note: The everyday Gulf hello — warmer and far more common than مرحبا. Usually doubled or intensified: هلا والله, يا هلا, هلا بك. It also works as the reply to هلا, so it is the one greeting you can never get wrong.
vocabulary.image_scene: A smiling young man in a white thobe raising his right hand in greeting at a doorway.
vocabulary.video_hint: The first word out of a host's mouth when a guest appears; vlog intros starting هلا والله.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The formal opener used by everyone, religious or not, when entering a room, a shop or a phone call. It is said by the person arriving. Learn it as one sound, not two words.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man stepping through an open door into a majlis, hand raised to his chest, others looking up.

example.english: Peace be upon you, Abu Khalid

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone entering a room or starting a video; street-interview openings.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The obligatory answer to السلام عليكم. Notice the words swap places. Not replying is a real slight, so this is the single most important reply in the lesson.
vocabulary.image_scene: Three men seated on floor cushions in a majlis turning toward the door and nodding in reply.
vocabulary.video_hint: The seated group answering an arrival; the reply is often chorused.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Used until roughly midday. In Saudi you will also hear the warmer يسعد صباحك (may your morning be happy). The first word carries the emphatic ص — let the a sound dark.
vocabulary.image_scene: Sunrise over flat rooftops and a minaret, a man on a balcony with a small coffee cup.
vocabulary.video_hint: Morning-routine vlogs; the opening line said to the camera or family at breakfast.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The fixed reply to صباح الخير. Never answer a good morning with another good morning — you answer with light. Note how الـ becomes in- before ن.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman in the kitchen turning around with a tray of tea glasses, smiling in reply.
vocabulary.video_hint: Second speaker in any morning exchange; family breakfast scenes.

vocabulary.teaching_note: From late afternoon onward — in practice, after the عصر prayer. Its reply is مساء النور, the same pattern as the morning pair, so you get two greetings for the price of one.
vocabulary.image_scene: Dusk on a corniche, string lights coming on, two friends meeting by the water.
vocabulary.video_hint: Evening gatherings and majlis arrivals after sunset.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'what is your colour'. This is the Kuwait–Bahrain–Qatar–Eastern Saudi form and is understood everywhere. To a woman: شلونك with -ik in Saudi, شلونج shloonich in Kuwait and the Emirates. Riyadh adds a و (وشلونك), the Emirates say شحالك, Jeddah says كيفك — all mean the same and all take the same reply.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two men mid-handshake, one leaning in with an inquiring, friendly expression.
vocabulary.video_hint: The second or third line of any greeting chain; listen for -ak vs -ich to hear the country.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The standard answer to شلونك. Even someone having a terrible day says this first. The bare الحمد لله on its own is also a complete answer — and it is the reply you will give a hundred times a week.
vocabulary.image_scene: A relaxed man giving a small thumbs-up and a nod, hand on chest.
vocabulary.video_hint: The answer to how-are-you in any interview or vlog greeting; often mumbled fast.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The host's welcome, said as you arrive and again as you are shown to a seat. Also used to mean 'you are welcome to come' when inviting. The reply is الله يحييك. Often shortened to حياك.
vocabulary.image_scene: A host at his door, arm extended inward, inviting a guest to enter a lit majlis.
vocabulary.video_hint: Hosts receiving guests; hospitality and majlis clips; also said to new viewers in vlog intros.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said to the person leaving; the person leaving answers الله يسلمك. In practice a Gulf goodbye is a small chain of its own: يالله … مع السلامة … الله يسلمك … في أمان الله. Young speakers also just say يالله باي.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man at a car door waving back toward a house where a family stands at the entrance.
vocabulary.video_hint: End of a visit or a phone call; vlog sign-offs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The friendly 'see you later', almost always with إن شاء الله in front of it. Note the first sound is n-shuuf — 'we see' — the same verb you will meet again in شوف (look).
vocabulary.image_scene: Two friends parting on a street corner, one turning back to wave.

example.arabic: إن شاء الله نشوفك على خير
example.transliteration: in shaaʾ allaah nshuufak ʿala khayr

vocabulary.video_hint: Closing lines of visits and vlogs; often paired with مع السلامة.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'what is your news'. It follows شلونك in the chain and takes the same reply. Every country has its version — شو الأخبار, وش أخبارك, and the Emirati شو اليديد (what's new) — but شخبارك is understood from Kuwait to Jeddah.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two women in abayas greeting each other at a mall entrance, one gesturing as if asking for news.
vocabulary.video_hint: Third line of a greeting chain; listen for it right after شلونك.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The two-syllable word that keeps the chain going: answer, then hand the question back. To a woman it is وإنتي w-inti. You will hear it before you learn the pronoun on its own in Lesson 4.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man pointing back politely at his friend, eyebrows raised, mid-conversation.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any two-way greeting; the hand-back after بخير.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.arabic: وعليكم السلام، هلا والله! حياك الله
dialogue.transliteration: w-ʿalaykum is-salaam, hala wallah! ḥayyaak allaah
dialogue.english: And upon you peace — hey there! Welcome

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: Fine, thank God — and you, how are things?

dialogue.speaker: Khalid
dialogue.english: God keep you — see you soon

sound_spotlight.explanation: The same greeting to a man ends in -ak; to a woman it ends in -ik in Saudi and -ich in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the Emirates. That ch is the single most audible clue to which country a speaker is from — hear it now, produce it later.

Two different h sounds. هلا has the ordinary English h. حياك and الحمد لله have the deep, breathy ح made by tightening the throat, like fogging a mirror. Mixing them up changes words, so listen for the difference first.
Gulf questions rise on the last syllable (shloo-NAK?) and the reply falls (il-ḥamdil-LAAH). Hearing the rise-then-fall helps you know when it is your turn to speak in a chain of greetings.

lesson_sequence.detail: A door opening onto a majlis. One line of English: greetings in the Gulf come in pairs; today you learn twelve and their replies. Tap يلّا.
Six greeting → reply pairs, each acted by two speakers on a split card. Native audio auto-plays greeting then reply; Arabic shown, English small underneath. Tap to replay either half.
Audio of a greeting plays; three replies appear as cards; tap the one that fits. Wrong taps replay the correct pair. Covers the six pairs plus شخبارك and نشوفك على خير.
The full dialogue plays with speakers highlighted line by line. Second pass: the learner taps when a turn changes hands.
Four replies only — وعليكم السلام, صباح النور, بخير الحمد لله, الله يسلمك — played and echoed by the learner with a simple record-and-compare bar. No score.
Twelve items, audio only: hear the greeting, tap the reply; hear the reply, tap the greeting. Missed items replay with both halves.
Words-learned counter rolls to 25. Nudge: say السلام عليكم to the next Arabic speaker you meet and listen for the reply.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you walk into a shop or an office where Arabic is spoken, say السلام عليكم and wait. Notice the reply comes back word for word.
real_world_prompts.context: Lesson-complete screen. Activates the first pair; the reply is guaranteed, so the learner cannot fail.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Listen to any Gulf vlog intro today and count the greetings before the vlogger says anything else. Two? Three? Four?
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day notification. Builds the expectation of a chain rather than a single hello.

real_world_prompts.prompt: If a tutor or friend asks شلونك؟, answer بخير الحمد لله and then hand it back with وإنت؟
real_world_prompts.context: Shown before a tutor session or conversation practice. The minimum viable chain: reply plus return.

video_needs.scene: Two people greeting at a door or on the street: the arrival says the peace greeting, the reply is audible, then شلونك / شخبارك and the handshake. Street-interview intros and hosts receiving guests are ideal.
